definition: Text segmentation is the process of dividing written text into meaningful units, such as words, sentences, or topics.
details: The term applies both to mental processes used by humans when reading text, and to artificial processes implemented in computers, which are the subject of natural language processing. The problem is non-trivial, because while some written languages have explicit word boundary markers, such as the word spaces of written English and the distinctive initial, medial and final letter shapes of Arabic, such signals are sometimes ambiguous and not present in all written languages. Compare speech segmentation, the process of dividing speech into linguistically meaningful portions.

explainer.lead: Text segmentation divides written text into meaningful units such as words, sentences or topics. It matters because some written languages lack clear boundary signals, making the split non-trivial.

tiers.eli5: It is like cutting a long strip of paper into pieces at the right places, where someone has forgotten to mark where each piece ends.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers segment text before tokenizing, sentence-splitting or topic analysis. The pitfall is that boundary signals are sometimes ambiguous — English word spaces and Arabic initial, medial and final letter shapes help, but not everywhere — and many written languages have no such markers at all.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally it is a partitioning of a text sequence into contiguous units according to a boundary criterion (word, sentence or topic). Limits stem from ambiguity of boundary signals and their absence in some writing systems, so no single rule generalizes across languages.

explainer.example: Splitting a paragraph into individual sentences, or a document into topic sections, before feeding the pieces to a model.
